detail.abstract: Artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) is acknowledged to provide incomes to tens of millions of individuals around the world, yet systematic data on miners’ earnings are lacking. We developed a sampling method and survey tools suited for systematic data collection and applied it to a stratified random sample of 453 miners in the largest mining town in Congo’s South Kivu province. Our research design allows us to study how much artisanal gold miners earn, and what determines their earnings. In doing so, we assess the financial attractiveness of artisanal mining, and uncover whether earnings from artisanal mining are merit-based, i.e. determined by experience, expertise and risk-taking behavior, or identity-based. This allows us to test the claim that artisanal mining has a social-levelling effect.

title: Data-Driven Contextual Pricing with Semi-Parametric Models
affiliations: Cornell University - Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management, Cornell University - Samuel Curtis Johnson Graduate School of Management and Cornell SC Johnson College of Business

detail.title: Data-Driven Contextual Pricing with Semi-Parametric Models
detail.abstract: We introduce a unified framework for the data-driven revenue-maximizing contextual pricing problem. Along with available contextual features, we consider two types of data: (1) observed customer valuations (also referred to as willingness-to-pay) and (2) customers’ binary purchase data and posted prices, without knowledge of the prior pricing policy. We assume a semi-parametric model of customer valuation with a log-linear function of contextual features and a distribution-free noise term. This model enables an elegant solution for the optimal pricing policy that separates the dependencies of the contextual features and the noise term. Leveraging this solution structure allows us to develop efficient algorithms for the above two data settings. We show asymptotic optimality and finite-sample performance guarantees for these algorithms under general, estimator-agnostic conditions. Finally, we conduct comprehensive numerical experiments with both synthetic and real data. Tested on synthetic data, our algorithms demonstrate superior performance with various underlying distributions of the noise term. Applied to a real-world online auto loan dataset, our algorithms outperform commonly adopted state-of-the-art benchmarks.

title: World Uncertainty Index for China and Stock Returns
affiliations: Wenzhou Business College

detail.title: World Uncertainty Index for China and Stock Returns
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the impact of the World Uncertainty Index for China proposed by Ahir, Bloom, and Furceri(2022) on the time series variation of Chinese stock market expected returns. Using this index, we find that a positive market risk premium compensates for the economic and politics uncertainty; a high uncertainty value predicts a subsequent high return. This predictability exists both in-and out-of-sample, and cannot be explained by extant Chinese economic and uncertainty measures. We exploit the underlying economic mechanism and demonstrate that the uncertainty index contains information about future Chinese household economic conditions and influences stock returns primarily through cash flow channels.

title: THE HIDDEN COST OF NOISE: How Hidden Organizational Sabotage Costs Your Company
affiliations: University of Portsmouth

detail.title: THE HIDDEN COST OF NOISE: How Hidden Organizational Sabotage Costs Your Company
detail.abstract:
What if your company's greatest enemy wasn't a competitor, but a set of behaviours you encourage every day? In 1944, as Allied forces sought to undermine Axis powers from within, the U.S. Office of Strategic Services (OSS)—the precursor to the CIA—issued a now-declassified handbook: the Simple Sabotage Field Manual. Designed for civilians in occupied territories, it revealed how to subtly disrupt enemy organizations without ever firing a shot.

The manual didn't call for explosives or cloak-and-dagger missions. Instead, it advised ordinary bureaucratic behaviours as powerful tools of sabotage. For example, it encouraged saboteurs to

Insist on doing everything through channels, Refer all matters to committees for further study and consideration, Bring up irrelevant issues as frequently as possible, Haggle over the precise wording of communications, Multiply the procedures and clearances involved in issuing instructions.

These tactics were designed to clog decision-making, sow confusion, and drain organizational energy—all without attracting suspicion. Eighty years later, these same behaviours thrive not in enemy organizations, but in modern corporations—often unintentionally. What the OSS once prescribed as deliberate sabotage has become, in many firms, standard operating procedure.

title: A New Digital Divide? Coder Worldviews, the "Slop Economy," and Democracy in the Age of AI
affiliations: University of Oslo - Centre for Development and the Environment and Peace Research Institute Oslo

detail.title: A New Digital Divide? Coder Worldviews, the "Slop Economy," and Democracy in the Age of AI

publicationDetails.detailsText: Accepted, Information, Communication, and Society

detail.abstract: Digital technologies are transforming democratic life in conflicting ways. This article bridges two perspectives to unpack these tensions. First, we present an original survey of software developers in Silicon Valley, interrogating how coders’ worldviews, ethics, and workplace cultures shape the democratic potential and social impact of the technologies they build. Results indicate that while most developers recognize the power of their products to influence civil liberties and political discourse, they often face ethical dilemmas and top-down pressures that can lead to design choices undermining democratic ideals. Second, we critically investigate these findings in the context of an emerging “new digital divide”, not of internet access but of information quality. We interrogate the survey findings in the context of the “slop economy”, in which billions of users unable to pay for high-quality content experience an internet dominated by low-quality, AI-generated ad-driven content. We find a reinforcing cycle between tech creator beliefs and the digital ecosystems they spawn. We discuss implications for democratic governance, arguing for more ethically informed design and policy interventions to help bridge the digital divide to ensure that technological innovation supports rather than subverts democratic values in the next chapter of the digital age.

title: Beyond OSBPs: assessing the feasibility of a "no-stop" border approach in Africa
affiliations: Desiderio Consultants Ltd.

detail.title: Beyond OSBPs: assessing the feasibility of a "no-stop" border approach in Africa
detail.abstract: The concept of "no-stop borders", where goods, people, and vehicles can cross frontiers without any stops for checks, has recently gained traction in Africa, raising strong interest in political and academic circles. This approach is increasingly explored as an aspirational goal able to enhance the economic integration of the continent, particularly in the context of the African Continental Free Trade Area. However, its realization remains largely theoretical, and its implementation is confronted by substantial impediments. Such a system necessitates significant institutional and political convergence among States, with a high degree of regulatory harmonization, enhanced frameworks for inter-agency cooperation and the adoption of sophisticated technological infrastructure: all aspects that in Africa are underdeveloped. A circumscribed application to selected "controlled" corridors for preapproved operators and goods within regions in Africa exhibiting a higher degree of economic integration (ex. Customs Unions), offers a more viable pathway for initial adoption of this approach.

title: Reconceiving the National Research Enterprise*
affiliations: Carnegie Mellon University - Engineering and Public Policy (EPP), MIT FutureTech, Indiana University - School of Informatics, Computing and Engineering and Georgia Institute of Technology

detail.title: Reconceiving the National Research Enterprise*

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no interests to declare. The views expressed here are those of the authors, individually, and do not necessarily represent those of their various institutions.

detail.abstract: U.S. leadership in scientific research is at a transformative moment. Not only is artificial intelligence playing a disruptive, even revolutionary, role, China has emerged as a viable competitor. As a source of U.S. competitive advantage, innovation, transformation, and diffusion is vital. Scientific knowledge must spread beyond its original research context and be applied to diverse problems. In these times of industrial revolution, universities play a central role, but funding should prioritize institutions that demonstrate effective diffusion and talent retention at national and regional levels. Given the priorities set by federal leadership, decentralized decision-making freedom allows institutions to experiment with solutions. While technical advantages are temporary, sustained leadership requires stable talent pathways that support continuous and rapid innovation that delivers value to end users faster than national competitors can innovate. U.S. scientific competitiveness depends not only on discovery but also on the diffusion and retention of tacit knowledge, particularly through graduate students who embody and transfer expertise. Talent attraction is a U.S. strength, but retention is equally critical since departing researchers can weaken the nation's competitive position by transferring tacit knowledge abroad. To succeed, the U.S. must compete globally to provide an attractive environment for scientists and incorporate retention as a metric of institutional success.

title: Re-establishing Public and Private Entrepreneurship in Knowledge-creating Frontier Innovation and Industrial Development

detail.title: Re-establishing Public and Private Entrepreneurship in Knowledge-creating Frontier Innovation and Industrial Development
detail.abstract: • Purpose: This study aims to reestablish both public and private entrepreneurship as the core of knowledge-creating innovation process that generates frontier industrial transformations. It is to bridge the research gap relating to the relinquishment of entrepreneurship as a commanding entity in knowledge-based innovation and industrial transformation studies, which is contrasting to factual industrial developments. • Methodology: The study augments Schumpeter's (1934) traditional approach of (without new knowledge) entrepreneur-led industrial transformation to include an open system of new knowledge creation and frontier (technology and industrial) development. The augmented "stylised process" framework is applied to cases of frontier industries and stages of open knowledge creation and commercialisation (as innovations and associated frontier industrial transformations). The data supporting case analyses are Chinese historyfriendly longitudinal data. • Findings: Applied to Chinese solar photovoltaic and mobile communication cases, the framework attests that entrepreneurship that creates, makes sufficient and commercialises technical knowledge in varied public and private organisations as innovations is the core driver of the transformations. All the cases are independent of simply prearranged knowledge systems and flows. • Implications for theory and practice: The above reestablishment of entrepreneurship accentuates to the top-level management the importance of strategic management of organisational entrepreneurship in all forms and sizes of public and private organisations. Competing at the frontier where required knowledge remains fluid, strategic entrepreneurship commanding the absorption and creation of knowledge through R&Ds is vital. The entrepreneurship constitute both necessary and sufficient conditions for commercialisation of such fluid knowledge as successive innovations. Setting policies on and providing supporting bases and/or systems for knowledge accumulations and flows are necessary but not sufficient for innovation commercialisation. Each type of entrepreneur could learn and compete for leading the frontier innovation diffusion process and exploit more profit through each (phase of) industrial transformation. Strategically, knowledge networks and IPRs grow essential for opportunity creation (by knowledge creation) and exploitation (by knowledge commercialisation) in frontier industries. • Originality and value: The study reestablishes entrepreneurship as a core concept of frontier knowledge-based industrial transformation. It also proposes a general entrepreneurship process model that accounts for the binding role of both public and private entrepreneurship in the transformation process.

title: Assyrian Entrepreneurship in Exile: Social Networks, Ethnic Capital, and Conflict Management in a Stateless Diaspora
affiliations: Royal Institute of Technology (KTH)

detail.title: Assyrian Entrepreneurship in Exile: Social Networks, Ethnic Capital, and Conflict Management in a Stateless Diaspora

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the research, analysis, or conclusions presented in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study did not involve human participants or experiments and therefore did not require ethics approval.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency, public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: Background: Assyrian * entrepreneurship in Sweden has developed under conditions shaped by exile, statelessness, and structural exclusion. While ethnic entrepreneurship has been widely studied, little is known about the specific experiences of stateless communities. This study explores how Assyrian entrepreneurs navigate both opportunity and marginalization within the Swedish institutional and economic landscape. Methods: The study is based on 20 in-depth interviews with Assyrian entrepreneurs in the Stockholm region, using a qualitative and phenomenological research approach. The analysis applies concepts such as mixed embeddedness, social capital, capital theory, and conflict management in diaspora settings. Results: Findings reveal that Assyrian entrepreneurs rely heavily on bonding social capital, informal financing, and transnational diaspora networks. Their entrepreneurship is shaped by experiences of mistrust toward formal institutions, gendered labor structures, and intergenerational tensions. Despite limited access to formal capital and support, they create resilient and communitybased economic systems that sustain cultural identity and autonomy. Conclusions: Assyrian entrepreneurship in exile is more than economic activity-it is a form of symbolic resistance, identity construction, and cultural continuity. The study contributes to ethnic entrepreneurship theory by integrating statelessness, conflict dynamics, and informal capital practices as key analytical dimensions.

title: Equitable Electricity Rate-Making in the Era of Distributed Energy: Balancing Risk and Efficiency
affiliations: , University of California, Santa Cruz - Department of Technology Management and National Graduate Institute for Policy Studies (GRIPS)

detail.title: Equitable Electricity Rate-Making in the Era of Distributed Energy: Balancing Risk and Efficiency
detail.abstract: Public Utility Commissions (PUCs) in several U.S. states face complex challenges in setting retail rates to balance equity, economic efficiency, and utility cost recovery, especially as distributed energy resources (DERs) become more prevalent. The growth of DERs has heightened the risk of a 'utility death spiral,' where increased DER adoption reduces traditional energy demand, prompting utilities to raise rates for remaining consumers. This situation can create equity issues, as consumers unable to adopt DERs will disproportionally bear the rising costs. This paper addresses these issues using a Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) approach, enabling PUCs to prioritize cost recovery while balancing equity and efficiency. Our findings show that pursuing a risk-averse rate design can mitigate deficits in cost recovery but may at the expense of worsening energy equity. This work highlights the need for a balanced ratemaking strategy that considers equity, risk, and efficiency in a DER-driven landscape.

title: Where has all the productivity gone? Italy's missing growth in the XXIst century: issues and pro-productivity policies
affiliations: and LUISS Lab of European Economics

detail.title: Where has all the productivity gone? Italy's missing growth in the XXIst century: issues and pro-productivity policies

declarations.funderStatement: The study was funded by The Productivity Institute, Manchester, UK

detail.abstract: Italy's economic growth has stagnated since the late 1990s, diverging from the trajectory of other advanced economies after decades of convergence driven by robust productivity gains. This paper examines the roots of Italy's persistent productivity slowdown in a historical, sectoral, and international context. It identifies weak MFP growth and capital deepening, particularly in intangible and digital assets, as well as underperformance in knowledge-intensive industries as critical contributors. Three self-reinforcing structural traps have hindered innovation, digital transformation, and efficient resource allocation: skills deficit, small scale of firms, and risk aversion. These traps, deeply rooted in Italy's economic and institutional fabric, have limited the country's ability to capitalize on globalization and technological change. Applying the Van Ark et al. (2023) policy framework, the paper reviews Italian productivity policies over the past forty years, highlighting a persistent pattern of fragmented, delayed, and ineffectively executed reforms. A policy agenda is sketched to unlock the structural traps and reposition Italy on a dynamic productivity path.

title: You go, I stay: intrahousehold evacuation behavior upon a disaster
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, and University of Antwerp - Institute of Development Policy and Management

detail.title: You go, I stay: intrahousehold evacuation behavior upon a disaster

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no conflict of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: We received positive travel advice for data collection from the High-Risk Destination Committee of the University of Antwerp (UA). The research received ethical clearance from the UA Ethical Advice Committee (file SHW_19_03).
declarations.funderStatement: This research was funded by Research Foundation Flanders (research project G029321N; scholarship 12W8320N) and the University of Antwerp’s Research Fund (DOCPRO – BOF scholarship FFB190256).

detail.abstract: Low-income countries are disproportionately affected by disasters, a situation that will worsen with global warming. Evacuation is an effective strategy to reduce the burden of disasters. Existing evacuation plans are however primarily based on studies conducted in high-income countries, ignoring contextual factors of low-income countries, such as large families with many children, low car ownership and high crime rates. We argue that these contextual factors give rise to partial evacuation, going against the long-held assumption in evacuation studies that households evacuate as a unit. To demonstrate this empirically, we study the evacuation behavior of almost 4,000 individuals from 500 households in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo, after the 2021 Nyiragongo volcano eruption. We rely on a structured survey and statistical analysis, complemented with narratives from open-ended interviews. Almost a third of households partially evacuated, leaving some members behind. Traditional gender roles largely determined who stayed behind or evacuated. Able women were more likely to evacuate, mostly on foot, to accompany children and the least mobile to safety, while able men and household heads were more likely to stay behind to protect property against looting. Our findings highlight the need to consider intra-household dynamics in evacuation behavior and design evacuation policies tailored to the specific context of low-income countries.

title: Predicting Effects, Missing Distributions: Evaluating LLMs as Human Behavior Simulators in Operations Management
affiliations: Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST), Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST) and Hong Kong University of Science & Technology (HKUST)

detail.title: Predicting Effects, Missing Distributions: Evaluating LLMs as Human Behavior Simulators in Operations Management
detail.abstract: LLMs are emerging tools for simulating human behavior in business, economics, and social science, offering a lower-cost complement to laboratory experiments, field studies, and surveys. This paper evaluates how well LLMs replicate human behavior in operations management. Using nine published experiments in behavioral operations, we assess two criteria: replication of hypothesis-test outcomes and distributional alignment via Wasserstein distance. LLMs reproduce most hypothesis-level effects, capturing key decision biases, but their response distributions diverge from human data, including for strong commercial models. We also test two lightweight strategies—Chain-of-Thought prompting and hyperparameter tuning—which reduce misalignment and can sometimes let smaller or open-source models match or surpass larger systems.

title: The Effect of Perceived Greenwashing on Consumer Trust and Brand Loyalty
affiliations: University of Cape Coast Ghana

detail.title: The Effect of Perceived Greenwashing on Consumer Trust and Brand Loyalty

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This an area of interest and I wasn't influenced by anybody.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This has no participants
declarations.funderStatement: I funded his work all by myself

detail.abstract: This paper examines the detrimental effects of perceived greenwashing on consumerbrand relationships. Specifically, it investigates how consumer perceptions of inauthentic environmental marketing influence brand trust and, subsequently, long-term brand loyalty. While prior studies have demonstrated that greenwashing damages trust, few have explored the mediating role of trust in loyalty models. The study is based on a comprehensive synthesis of existing scholarly literature in the fields of marketing, consumer behavior, and business ethics. It analyzes theoretical frameworks and empirical findings to build a cohesive argument on the causal chain linking greenwashing to negative behavioral outcomes. The analysis reveals a strong consensus in the literature: perceived greenwashing functions as a significant breach of consumer trust. This erosion of trust is identified as the primary mediator that leads to a decline in brand loyalty, reduced purchase intent, and an increase in negative word-of-mouth. The research also highlights that while high pre-existing loyalty may offer a temporary buffer, the long-term consequences of deceptive environmental claims are consistently negative across various industries. The findings carry significant implications for marketing practice, underscoring the strategic necessity of authentic and transparent communication regarding sustainability initiatives. For theory, the paper reinforces the centrality of trust as a foundational element in loyalty models, particularly within the context of corporate social responsibility. It concludes that in an era of heightened consumer skepticism, the reputational and financial risks associated with greenwashing far outweigh any potential short-term benefits.

title: Distant Imaging: A Six-Phase Framework for AI Co-Creation in Marketing Education
affiliations: ISTEC Business School, Tongji University and ISTEC Business School

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable

detail.abstract: Marketing education needs to prepare students for a profession increasingly dominated by AI-generated visual content while stimulating human creative agency. This paper introduces "distant imaging"-a six-phase framework extending Floridi's concept of "distant writing" to visual domains, positioning AI-generated imagery as raw material for creative meaning-making. Grounded in constructivist pedagogy, the framework acknowledges the shift from aspirational to authentic marketing and the trend to content co-creation with Generative AI. Through hands-on studio activities progressing from individual experimentation to collaborative interpretation and professional application, students develop competencies for creative partnership with AI while maintaining human agency, critical awareness, and ethical responsibility Kelley & Kelley, 2013). The framework offers marketing educators a detailed pedagogical roadmap for integrating GenAI tools while developing rather than diminishing student creativity.

title: Board Gender Diversity Reforms and Corporate Environmental and Social Misconduct
affiliations: EDHEC Business School, affiliation not provided to SSRN and IESEG School of Management

detail.title: Board Gender Diversity Reforms and Corporate Environmental and Social Misconduct
detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the increase in female representation on corporate boards serves as an effective monitor of environmental and social (E&S) misconduct. Using the staggered adoption of board gender diversity reforms in the U.S., we find that a greater presence of women on boards is associated with a decrease in E&S misconduct. This effect is primarily driven by female non-executive directors, particularly those who are not overextended. Moreover, greater female representation on E&S committees is linked to lower levels of E&S misconduct. Importantly, all these effects are more pronounced for social misconduct than for environmental misconduct, highlighting the emphasis that female directors place on addressing social issues.

title: Innovation in Polybutadiene–PET Composite Materials Derived from Used Tires and Plastics for Sustainable Concrete: Socio-Environmental Impacts
affiliations: University of Maroua and University of Yaoundé1

detail.title: Innovation in Polybutadiene–PET Composite Materials Derived from Used Tires and Plastics for Sustainable Concrete: Socio-Environmental Impacts

declarations.ethicsApproval: In studies with participants, ethics approval has be given.

detail.abstract: The growing challenge of sustainable management of plastic waste and used tires, particularly in tropical and Sahelian urban areas, calls for innovative solutions that simultaneously reduce environmental impacts and valorize materials. This research investigates the integration of polybutadiene-PET (PB-PET) composites, derived from recycled PET plastics and end-of-life tires, as partial substitutes for mineral aggregates in cementclay matrices for concrete. The experimental approach involved incorporating various proportions of PET, crumb rubber, and hybrid formulations, while considering the effect of surface pre-treatments (NaOH, silane, plasma) on adhesion properties. Mechanical (compression, flexural, tensile), physical (density, durability under freeze-thaw cycles and acidic or saline environments), and microstructural performances were comparatively assessed against a control concrete. Results indicate that moderate PET incorporation (≈5%) preserves or even enhances mechanical strengths, whereas rubber significantly reduces them. Hybrid formulations, particularly when combined with surface pre-treatments, provide a satisfactory compromise through improved interfacial cohesion. Finally, the addition of polybutadiene (1-3%) increases toughness and energy absorption capacity. Overall, a 10-15% PB-PET substitution emerges as the optimal option, balancing socioeconomic viability, technical performance, and durability, thereby offering relevant prospects for sustainable construction and circular economy in tropical and Sahelian contexts.

title: IMPACT OF CONSUMER HEURISTIC BEHAVIOUR AND SOCIAL MEDIA MARKETING ON BRAND CHOICE: EVIDENCE FROM ORGANIC PRODUCTS IN THANJAVUR DISTRICT
