detail.abstract: To meet the rising demand for minerals, mining companies have ventured into fragile areas, often at the expense of artisanal miners. This has led to grievances, and at times violence. Who among the aggrieved intend to use violence? How can peace be maintained? This paper uses individual-level data to address these questions. Among a sample of 469 about-to-be-evicted artisanal miners in Eastern Congo, we inquire about the intention to engage in several forms of violence. We identify how this intention varies with miners’ past exposure to violence and attitudes towards policies that seek social peace. A large proportion of miners intends to destroy the company’s property, attack its employees, use fire arms, or join an armed group. These would-be-fighters are motivated by grievances, as well as material and social incentives. Our results contribute to understanding the micro-motivations underpinning the local resource curse and entail concrete lessons for mining policies.

title: Academic Silence in Science Publishing: Authority, Conformity, and Censorship
affiliations: Shenyang Normal University

detail.title: Academic Silence in Science Publishing: Authority, Conformity, and Censorship
detail.abstract: Scientific progress relies on open inquiry and the free critique of prevailing theories. However, a mounting body of evidence suggests that criticism of dominant paradigms and institutional authorities is often stifled in contemporary academia. This review examines how social and procedural pressures create "academic silence" in scientific publishing. We discuss psychological factors (authority bias, conformity pressure, and fear of ostracism) that discourage dissent. We then analyze structural mechanisms-peer-review gatekeeping, editorial bias, and the invocation of privacy or conflict-of-interest rules-that systematically filter out critical analyses and error-corrections. For example, journals and preprint servers have invoked data-protection laws (e.g. GDPR) and conflictof-interest disclosures as justifications to reject manuscripts that challenge mainstream findings. Such practices create "silence zones" where fundamental problems go unaddressed, undermining the epistemic integrity of science. We synthesize empirical studies showing widespread self-censorship (e.g. surveys of faculty fearing sanctions for controversial research) and document recent cases of mass retractions and "paper mills" that signal a broader publishing crisis. The review concludes that without reforms to promote transparency, protect whistleblowers, and realign incentives, the cumulative effect is a weakening of scientific accountability and innovation. We call for clearer standards on disclosure (balancing transparency with privacy), and for publishers to safeguard editorial independence so that critical scholarship can survive peer review.

title: The PvP Disclosures Show Problems in U.S. Executive Pay
affiliations: Shareholder Value Advisors, Inc.

detail.title: The PvP Disclosures Show Problems in U.S. Executive Pay
detail.abstract: The conventional wisdom in U.S. executive pay is that maintaining a target pay percentile with a high percent of pay at risk achieves the three basic objectives of executive pay. Not letting target pay fall below the median retains key talent, not letting target pay rise above the median limits shareholder cost and a high percent of pay at risk ensures a strong incentive. The new Pay Versus Performance (PvP) data provides the data-"mark to market" pay-to test the conventional wisdom. Individual company regressions relating relative mark to market pay to relative TSR quantify incentive strength (slope), alignment (correlation) and performance adjusted cost (the intercept). These regressions show that the conventional wisdom only works for about 15% of companies. To help understand the weaknesses of the conventional wisdom, I show that that there is a simple pay plan with annual grants of performance shares that provides a perfect correlation of relative pay and relative TSR and that this perfect correlation pay plan di ers from conventional practice in two ways. First, it says that target pay should be market pay adjusted for trailing relative performance, not market pay regardless of past performance. Second, it says that vesting should take out the industry component of the stock return, not use company performance to leverage industry performance as plans with relative TSR vesting do. The perfect correlation plan shows that mark to market pay should be equal to the expected future value of cumulative market pay plus a fixed and symmetric share of the excess return. It shows how to improve executive pay by combining fixed sharing-the guiding concept of executive pay before World War II-with competitive pay levels-the guiding concept of executive pay since World War II.

title: Bullshit and Organization Studies
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Copenhagen Business School and Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Bullshit and Organization Studies
detail.abstract: Bullshit is a ubiquitous communication practice that permeates many dimensions of organizational life. This essay outlines different understandings of bullshit and discusses their significance in the context of organization studies. While it is tempting to reject bullshit as corrosive to rational organizational practice, we argue that it is necessary to understand its organizational significance and performative nature more systematically. We outline different social functions of bullshit focusing on two particular types of managerial practices in which bullshit is likely to play a significant role: commanding and strategizing. On this backdrop, we consider bullshit in terms of the messages, senders and receivers involved, focusing especially on the dynamics between these dimensions in the context of organizations. The final part of this essay debates the reasons why bullshit, which is recognized by organizational members, is rarely called and rejected explicitly.

title: Intersection of AI-Driven Arbitration and Mediation Methods with the New York Convention (1958): A Legal Analysis
affiliations: Sindh Bar Council

detail.title: Intersection of AI-Driven Arbitration and Mediation Methods with the New York Convention (1958): A Legal Analysis

keywords: Article V of the New York Convention

detail.abstract: This research examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI)-based arbitration and mediation methods and the New York Convention 1958, focusing on the challenges and opportunities arising from the incorporation of large language models (LLMs) into international commercial arbitration. While AI tools offer increased efficiency, convenience, and the potential for predictive analysis, their use also raises important legal issues, including concerns about procedural fairness, public order, and procedural efficiency under Article V of the New York Convention. Specific risks include methodological bias, uncertain decision-making, and uncertainty about liability. The research paper argues that a hybrid model, where AI complements but does not replace human arbitrators, is the way forward. The study proposes a series of reforms/recommendations to ensure fair trial and enforcement, including clear arbitration rules, accreditation standards, transparency, and data protection measures. It also highlights the need for a balanced approach that fully exploits the potential of artificial intelligence while preserving the fundamental principles of fairness and party autonomy.

title: Strategic Aging and the Paradox of Food Waste Fees in Decentralized Supply Chains
affiliations: Department of Logistics, Kühne Logistics University, Neoma Business School and Kühne Logistics University

detail.title: Strategic Aging and the Paradox of Food Waste Fees in Decentralized Supply Chains

declarations.funderStatement: This research has been funded by the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foun- dation) under the Project ID: TR 1496/1-1.

detail.abstract:
Problem definition: Retailers often implement Minimum Life on Receipt (MLOR) requirements and FIFO issuing policies to ensure product freshness and reduce waste. However, in decentralized supply chains where manufacturers set wholesale prices, these practices may shift waste upstream and impact overall profitability. Moreover, the effectiveness of waste-related policy interventions is unclear when retailers do not control all contract terms. This study investigates how retailers should combine MLOR requirements and issuing policies under stochastic demand and manufacturer pricing power, highlighting the trade-offs between food waste fees, operational choices, profitability, service level, and environmental outcomes. 

Methodology/results: We develop a game-theoretic model of a decentralized two-echelon supply chain managing a product with a short, fixed shelf life. The retailer chooses whether to impose MLOR and whether to apply FIFO or LIFO, while the manufacturer sets the wholesale price. Both parties determine their base stocks. The model incorporates lost sales, endogenous pricing, and asymmetric waste costs. Using analytical and numerical methods, we characterize equilibrium outcomes. Key findings include: (i) manufacturers optimally ship the most aged units permitted, (ii) relaxing MLOR can benefit retailers by lowering wholesale prices, even if only aged goods are received, (iii) raising waste costs does not always reduce total waste, as it can trigger policy shifts with unintended consequences, and (iv) these shifts can, in some cases, improve service levels by encouraging higher inventory levels. 

Managerial implications: MLOR and FIFO policies do not universally lower waste or improve profit. Retailers must carefully evaluate when these practices are beneficial, as strict MLOR requirements can backfire by shifting inefficiencies upstream. Policymakers should avoid one-size-fits-all waste penalties and instead consider moderate, well-calibrated fees across the supply chain. Effective waste reduction and supply chain performance require aligning incentives across firms through a holistic, context-sensitive approach.

title: Politics, Governance, and Leadership: What Can we Learn from the Academy of Management's Response to EO13769?
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, Boston University - Department of Organizational Behavior, Cornell University, University of Alberta - Department of Strategic Management and Organization, Northeastern University, University of Minnesota - Minneapolis, Insper Institute of Education and Research, University of Massachusetts Boston, Dublin Institute of Technology, Copenhagen Business School, Arizona State University, Fordham University and University of Utah

detail.title: Politics, Governance, and Leadership: What Can we Learn from the Academy of Management's Response to EO13769?
detail.abstract: Organization design seeks to balance potentially conflicting objectives while achieving a broader mission. EO13769 created a challenge for the president of the Academy of Management in leading through these conflicts, as President Anita McGahan describes: how to be true to her own moral values while leading an organization with well-established design constraints, and members with diverse opinions. This article shares the perspectives of 12 scholars on the lessons we can learn from Professor McGahan's leadership of a constraining organization through a challenging time.

title: Moral Philosophy and Archetypes in the Symbolic Cohesion of the Story Mirringa Mirronga
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS and Independent

detail.title: Moral Philosophy and Archetypes in the Symbolic Cohesion of the Story Mirringa Mirronga
detail.abstract: The analysis of Rafael Pombo’s La Mirringa Mirronga reveals how Colombian children’s literature goes beyond entertainment to become a moralizing tool and a means of social cohesion. Through the figure of the “deontological villain,” the tale illustrates the breach of fundamental duties and the necessity of punishment as a reaffirmation of the norm, in line with Kantian ethics. Similarly, the representation of the “anti-villain” shows how fear, interpreted through Machiavelli and Hobbes, works as a mechanism of social control and the preservation of communal and ecological order. The work highlights the pedagogical power of storytelling in transmitting universal and collective values.

title: Environmental Awareness Factors that Influence Pro-Environmental Behavior of Tourism Students at UNASAM, Huaraz, 2025
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Santiago Antunez de Mayolo and Universidad Nacional Santiago Antunez de Mayolo

detail.title: Environmental Awareness Factors that Influence Pro-Environmental Behavior of Tourism Students at UNASAM, Huaraz, 2025
detail.abstract: The study aimed to determine the influence of environmental awareness factors (environmental knowledge, perception, and motivation) on the pro-environmental behavior of Tourism students at UNASAM, Huaraz, 2025. A quantitative methodology with a non-experimental cross-sectional design was employed, using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to analyze causal relationships between constructs. The sample consisted of 152 students from the aforementioned program, selected through simple random sampling. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire with 5-point Likert scales, validated through confirmatory factor analysis, AVE, and Fornell & Larcker discriminant analysis. Results revealed that environmental knowledge does not significantly influence environmental awareness (β = 0.159, p = 0.195), while environmental perception (β = 0.243, p = 0.031) and environmental motivation (β = 0.333, p = 0.005) present significant and positive effects. Environmental awareness proved to be an extremely significant predictor of pro-environmental behavior (β = 0.906, p = 0.000), explaining 82.1% of its variance. It is concluded that environmental motivation is the most influential factor on environmental awareness, and that the latter acts as a fundamental mediator between cognitive-affective factors and concrete conservation actions. Findings suggest that to train environmentally responsible tourism professionals, it is more effective to develop environmental perceptions and motivations than to solely provide theoretical knowledge.

title: Large and Nimble or Compact and Cohesive? A Multi-Faceted Exploration of Capabilities and Complementarities for Business Model Innovation and Performance
affiliations: Ozyegin University

detail.title: Large and Nimble or Compact and Cohesive? A Multi-Faceted Exploration of Capabilities and Complementarities for Business Model Innovation and Performance
detail.abstract: This study employs a configurational approach to business model innovation (BMI) and firm performance to resolve several issues pertaining to theory and practice. First, within the research stream that links BMI to antecedents and outcomes, there is little systematic evidence about the role of interfirm complementarities and the performance implications. Second, this body of research has predominantly focused on linear models. This approach overlooks the inherent complexity in the phenomenon regarding multiple pathways and asymmetric relationships. To address these issues, the interplay of (i) strategic agility as the internal capability for BMI and (ii) structural embeddedness, which accounts for integrated interfirm complementarities, is explored in the effective pursuit of BMI in both large firms and SMEs in service industries. Findings from the fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis on 77 firms reveal that integrated interfirm complementarities substitute internal capabilities in enabling BMI and performance in the SME context. For large firms, these complementarities may act as a barrier to attaining the outcomes, while strategic agility provides immunity to these influences. The study augments existing theories to resolve the issues as called for by earlier studies and provides a nuanced picture that relates conceptual discussions to practical challenges.

detail.title: ALGORITHMIC EXCLUSION BY LARGE LANGUAGE MODELS *
detail.abstract: This paper explores whether large language models (LLMs) can learn predatory strategies in dynamic environments in which an incumbent faces repeated entry threat. Using Ope-nAI's GPT-4.1 as decision-making agents, we find that LLMs learn to predate when both predation and accommodation are theoretically viable, and adopt aggressive strategies when only accommodation is theoretically viable. Further, profit optimization is limited, highlighting both strategic learning and its limitations.

title: Endogenous Timing in an International Mixed Duopoly with a Foreign Labor-Managed Competitor
affiliations: Institute for Economic Sciences

detail.title: Endogenous Timing in an International Mixed Duopoly with a Foreign Labor-Managed Competitor
detail.abstract: This paper considers an international mixed duopoly model in which a state-owned public firm competes against a foreign labor-managed firm. The paper investigates endogenous roles of the firms by adopting the observable delay game and shows that the state-owned public firm should never play the role of Staclkelberg leader.

title: Beyond Benefits Realization: Towards a Framework for Sustaining and Enhancing Project Benefits
affiliations: Riphah International University,  and Riphah International University

detail.title: Beyond Benefits Realization: Towards a Framework for Sustaining and Enhancing Project Benefits
detail.abstract:
Purpose – This study examines the processes of benefits sustainment and enhancement in non-governmental organization (NGO) projects, emphasizing their critical importance for ensuring long-term value creation beyond project delivery.

Design/methodology/approach – This study utilizes semi-structured interviews with high-level decision-makers in NGOs to understand the concepts of benefits sustainment and enhancement as well as how these concepts manifest in practice.

Findings – The study identifies eight themes categorized into three core dimensions underpinning benefits sustainment and enhancement: strategic foresight and purpose, synergistic stakeholder collaboration, and a prospecting mindset coupled with sustained governance engagement. These dimensions highlight the importance of adaptability, stakeholder co-creation, and iterative governance in navigating the complexities of dynamic project environments and ensuring long-term impact.

Originality/value – This study extends the discourse on benefits realization to the important but underexplored stages of benefits sustainment and enhancement. Drawing on projects-as-practice and dynamic systems theory, it highlights the importance of adopting a complex adaptive systems approach at the ‘back-end’ of projects and develops a novel framework that captures the interplay of strategic foresight, stakeholder collaboration, and sustained governance engagement in ensuring long-term project value.

Practical implications – The study provides actionable insights for NGO leaders and project managers. It emphasizes the need for enduring governance systems, stakeholder collaboration, and adaptability to evolving contexts. The findings can inform strategies for enhancing project sustainability and long-term social impact in dynamic and resource-constrained environments.

detail.title: Revisiting the Principal-Agent Framework in the Context of Projects: Drawing Parallels with Corporate Governance

publicationDetails.detailsText: Project Management Journal, volume 56, issue 1, 2025[10.1177/87569728241270572]

detail.abstract: This paper examines the principal-agent framework in the context of projects and contrasts it with its corporate governance roots. Drawing on the theory of the firm as a nexus of contracts, it conceptualizes organizations and projects as nexuses of multi-level, intra-and inter-organizational, principal-principal and principal-agent relationships. Subsequently, the characteristics of the nexus of relationships in corporations are contrasted with those in three project archetypes, and the implications for project governance are discussed. This paper highlights that the principal-agent framework offers fertile avenues for further research and advocates for a concerted effort to indigenize the framework to the project context.

detail.title: Examining the Impact of Creative Accounting Practices on Financial Performance of Financial Institutions: A Case Study of Listed Commercial Banks in Nigeria

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Authors affirm that no conflicting interest that could influence the study was found.
declarations.ethicsApproval: None of such in the paper.

detail.abstract: The underlying consequences of creative accounting make it a dangerous path which has resulted in financial crisis of many top-rank organizations over the years. Many studies have been carried out on creative accounting but have not involved unresolved complaints which are the gap this study tries to fill by examining the impact of creative accounting on financial performance of commercial banks in Nigeria for the period 2020-2024. Ex-post facto research design was used, ensuring that publicly available data was gathered on the independent variable (Unresolved Complaints) and the dependent variables (ROE, ROA, and NIM). The Auto-Regression Distributed Lag models (ARDL) and Bounds Test in the E-Views (version 10) were used for data analysis. It was found out that creative accounting has a significant relationship with financial performance in both the short-run and long-run. The study, however, recommended that banks should investigate unresolved complaints using the internal auditor forming a coalition with other factors to improve financial performance.

title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Aging Cheese Inventory Management under Correlated Prices
affiliations: Technische Universität München (TUM), Technical University of Munich, Technical University of Munich and Technische Universität München (TUM)

detail.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Aging Cheese Inventory Management under Correlated Prices
detail.abstract: In aging cheese inventory management, producers must account for auto-regressive and correlated prices, both for raw milk at the purchasing side and for age-differentiated final products at the sales market side. Purchasing decisions determine the youngest additions to the multi-age inventory system. In production decisions, amelioration effects entail a trade-off between immediate revenues and further maturation. Producers have operational flexibility in issuance decisions because the age printed on the packaging represents only the minimum maturation time, allowing for deliberate excess. We solve the aging cheese inventory problem using deep reinforcement learning (DRL), as the problem size grows exponentially with the number of inventory age classes. However, state-of-the-art actor-critic DRL algorithms face difficulties when dealing with the high-dimensional action spaces induced by issuance flexibility. We introduce and analyze three possible remedies. First, we consider action space dimensionality reduction by curtailing issuance flexibility. The second approach also reduces dimensionality via actor pipelining, allowing issuance actions to be replaced with heuristic rules. Third, we analyze multi-agent actor architectures that distribute learning across multiple neural networks. Our results show that dimensionality reduction via pipelining achieves the best trade-off between policy quality and computational effort. Overall, action dimensionality reduction is both more effective and more efficient than multi-agent designs. Compared to a myopic rolling-horizon planning benchmark, our DRL policies increase profits by 16.7%, on average. Moreover, modeling the cheese-specific price dynamics is essential. Policies trained under simplified price assumptions yield profit losses of 6.7%, on average. In full factorial experiments, we investigate the effect of key price process parameters: mean reversion speed, volatility, and correlation of purchase and sales prices. In contrast to prior work, we find that issuance flexibility provides notable profit gains only in highly volatile, fast mean-reverting price environments.

title: Smoggy Spending: The Impact of Air Pollution on Offline Cashless Spending
affiliations: PBCSF, Tsinghua University, School of Finance, Nankai University and PBCSF, Tsinghua University

detail.title: Smoggy Spending: The Impact of Air Pollution on Offline Cashless Spending
detail.abstract: This paper studies how air pollution shapes offline cashless spending in China. Using monthly transaction data from 118,698 merchants across 332 cities (2019-2023), matched with air quality and weather records, we track sales, transactions, customer counts, and payment structures. We find that higher pollution unexpectedly stimulates consumption: a 10-point increase in the Air Quality Index raises sales, transactions, and customer counts by about 1%. Instrumental variable and regression discontinuity designs confirm a causal effect. The increase comes mainly from more frequent but smaller purchases and greater participation by new customers. Effects are strongest in food, services, and non-durable goods, while durables respond little. These results reveal a new behavioral channel through which environmental conditions influence local commerce, showing that poor air quality can reallocate spending patterns in cashless economies.

title: When to Innovate and When to Imitate
affiliations: University of Michigan, Stephen M. Ross School of Business, Harvard University and Harvard University

detail.title: When to Innovate and When to Imitate
detail.abstract: While innovation is widely celebrated as a path to competitive advantage, many firms fail because they pursue innovation when imitation would be more effective.  This article presents a framework for determining whether companies should innovate or imitate based on two dimensions: industry maturity and competitive position.  In nascent industries with unexplored opportunities, innovation typically succeeds by discovering new market spaces.  However, in mature industries where most territory has been mapped, firms often benefit more from imitating nearby, better-performing competitors within their “imitation radius”—the zone of feasible catch-up.  Companies at the industry frontier should innovate, while those behind should strategically imitate.  The framework guides organizational implementation through structure, talent, processes, and timing adjustments tailored to each strategy.  By recognizing that imitation can be a legitimate strategic choice rather than a failure, managers can make more informed decisions about resource allocation and competitive positioning.

detail.abstract: In September 2024, Australia introduced mandatory minimum age classifications for video games containing gambling-like mechanics, including loot boxes and simulated gambling. This study investigates compliance with the new scheme across the 100 top-grossing mobile games on the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Our analysis reveals widespread noncompliance, with 20 games on the Apple App Store and 48 on the Google Play Store failing to meet classification requirements. These findings highlight critical shortcomings in enforcement, platform accountability, and regulatory clarity. We argue that the current classification framework is ill-suited to the realities of contemporary digital game distribution, and offer policy recommendations to strengthen consumer protection against gambling-like content in games.

title: How does ENSO Impact U.S. Oil Spot and Future Prices?

detail.title: How does ENSO Impact U.S. Oil Spot and Future Prices?

keywords: Oil Futures and Goods Market Price

detail.abstract: This paper examines the impact of El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) shocks on U.S. oil futures and goods market prices from 1983:03 to 2024:10 via the Time-Varying Parameter Local Projections (TVP-LP) model. By allowing impulse responses to evolve over time, we capture dynamic shifts in the oil market's sensitivity to El Niño and La Niña events across different time-horizons. Our findings reveal an asymmetric response, where El Niño shocks exhibit a negative effect on oil futures and goods market prices, while La Niña shocks-especially extreme ones-lead to persistent upward price pressures. The effect becomes more pronounced at horizons within 12 months, indicating delayed transmission mechanisms through supply chain disruptions and changes in global energy demand. Additionally, the response intensifies in extreme ENSO episodes, highlighting non-linearities in climate-driven oil price fluctuations.

title: Right Price, Right Time: Fulfillment Decisions for Online Retail
affiliations: Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE) - Department of Industrial Engineering and Innovation Sciences, Eindhoven University of Technology, Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE) and Eindhoven University of Technology (TUE) - Department of Industrial Engineering and Innovation Sciences

detail.title: Right Price, Right Time: Fulfillment Decisions for Online Retail
detail.abstract: Consumers' purchasing decisions from online channels mainly depend on two critical factors; the selling price and the delivery lead time. Fast deliveries and more affordable prices might result in higher demand and higher revenues, but might also complicate last-mile delivery operations. Retailers face a major challenge of setting options that trigger enough demand and ensure high profitability. Each option is a combination of a selling price and a delivery lead time. In this study, we tackle this challenge. We consider a retailer selling a product through its online channel. The demand is random and customers' purchasing behavior is characterized by their reservation prices. We propose three policies differing in how flexibly they adjust price and lead time over the season: (i) a static M-option policy that fixes up to M specifications at the start and dynamically chooses which subset to offer based on inventory; (ii) a dynamic policy that offers one or two options and re-specifies them each period as inventory changes; and (iii) a hybrid policy that commits to one static option and adds a dynamically adjustable second option when beneficial.We develop value-iteration algorithms, analyze structural properties, and provide exact and heuristic optimization methods. We find that offering more options and allowing their specifications to vary over time significantly improves profitability, especially when costs are high, inventory is limited, or customer sensitivity to delivery lead time is strong. However, the benefit of additional dynamic options decreases as the selling season gets longer, suggesting that flexibility is most valuable in short-term or high-uncertainty settings.

title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in International Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) Processes: Challenges and Possibilities
affiliations: Sindh Bar Council

detail.title: Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in International Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) Processes: Challenges and Possibilities
detail.abstract: This study aims to understand how AI can best be integrated into arbitration, identifying its potential benefits in improving the efficiency and consistency of dispute resolution mechanisms and overcoming obstacles such as lack of understanding, clarity and accountability in AI-based decision-making processes. This study uses a theoretical legal research method based on legal principles, norms and laws. The research process consists of two stages, firstly, conducting legal research to achieve legal objectives. Secondly, obtaining secondary information through a critical review of the law. This study uses a legal approach based on relevant laws and regulations. Data sources include books, journals and other relevant legal documents. In order to better understand the legal framework related to Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR), the New York Convention and the UNCITRAL Model Law were prioritized to identify and analyse specific legal norms. By overcoming existing limitations and developing an appropriate regulatory framework, the efficiency and quality of AI-based dispute resolution processes can be effectively improved. This will ultimately benefit society and support the development of the dispute resolution sector.

detail.abstract: Does moving to a new environment change people's cultural thought style? We tracked the cultural thought style of 1,462 university students at 18 sites over time after they moved across China for college. We tested their holistic thought, which is more common in interdependent cultures. One logical prediction is that students would think less holistically after moving to big cities and more economically developed areas, in line with modernization theory. However, moving to bigger cities or more developed areas did not predict decreases in holistic thought. Instead, regions' history of rice versus wheat farming predicted change in thought style. Within just five months, students who moved to wheat-farming prefectures thought less holistically than people who moved to rice-farming prefectures. This fits with the idea that rice farming required more coordination and interdependence than wheat farming. In a follow-up wave three years later, differences widened between students in rice and wheat areas. This three-wave longitudinal study documents the transmission of cultural differences in cognition, even without personal experience farming. The results suggest that China's farming history is still shaping cultural differences in the modern day.

title: ICT Usage and Competitive Strategies in Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Jamaica
affiliations: Unversity of the Commonwealth Caribbean, Unversity of the Commonwealth Caribbean, , Unversity of the Commonwealth Caribbean, Unversity of the Commonwealth Caribbean and Unversity of the Commonwealth Caribbean

detail.title: ICT Usage and Competitive Strategies in Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises in Jamaica
detail.abstract: MSMEs are a significant medium for stimulating growth and social development in the local economy. The purpose of this study was to investigate and gain an understanding of the levels of ICT usage, the factors influencing ICT adoption, and the strategies MSMEs employed to achieve competitive advantage in Jamaica. The study also determined the relationship between competitive strategies and the level of ICT Usage in MSMEs. This research adopted a descriptive approach consisting of quantitative methodologies that employed a survey design using a self-administered questionnaire. The research explored three concepts: these are ICT Usage, Competitive Strategies and ICT Factors-Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The sample size comprised of 220 MSMEs in the parishes of St. Catherine, St. Thomas, Kingston and St. Andrew. We conducted a series of multiple regression models using the data we obtained. The finding suggests that there is an average usage of ICT by businesses, of which E-commerce is the most highly used among the MSME. A high percentage of businesses reported that Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) was likely to impact their adoption of ICT.

title: Why VAT Pass-Through Varies Across Countries: The Role of Market Power
affiliations: Stockholm University - Institute for International Economic Studies (IIES), Nova School of Business and Economics, Danmarks Nationalbank (The Central Bank of Denmark) and Nova School of Business and Economics

detail.title: Why VAT Pass-Through Varies Across Countries: The Role of Market Power
detail.abstract: We show that VAT pass-through rates depend systematically on market concentration using data from 16 European countries covering 1999-2019. Low-concentration industries exhibit 40% contemporaneous pass-through to consumers, while highconcentration industries show near-zero transmission. Crosscountry differences explain 72% of the variation in market concentration. This heterogeneity accounts for 16% of crosscountry variation in pass-through rates.

title: Corporations as Political Actors - A Report on the First Swiss Master Class in Corporate Social Responsibility
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School, Baur Consulting, affiliation not provided to SSRN, American University, Queen Mary University of London, Brown University - Department of Political Science, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - RSM Erasmus University, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Corporations as Political Actors - A Report on the First Swiss Master Class in Corporate Social Responsibility
detail.abstract: This paper presents a report on the first Swiss Master Class in Corporate Social Responsibility, which was held between the 8th and 9th December 2006 at HEC Lausanne in Switzerland. The first section of the report introduces the topic of the master class – ‚Corporations as Political Actors – Facing the Postnational Challenge’ – as well as the concept of the master class. The second section gives an overview of papers written by nine young scholars that were selected to present their research. The brief summary of each paper also includes a summary of comments from the masters, practitioners, and NGO representatives at the event. The third section brings in the perspectives of one master and one NGO representative on the discussed issues. The final section offers a brief wrap-up of the discussed topics and outlines ways to structure future conceptual and empirical research.

title: Beyond the Liberal/Non-Liberal: Reclaiming Secularism in the Palestinian Society
affiliations: Sapir Academic College

detail.title: Beyond the Liberal/Non-Liberal: Reclaiming Secularism in the Palestinian Society
detail.abstract: In August 2019, the local council of Umm al-Fahem, Israel, cancelled a scheduled performance of the known Palestinian rapper Tamer Nafar, claiming that Nafar's artistic work did not meet with the town's accepted religious, moral, and social norms. Subsequently, residents of the town and the Association for Civil Rights in Israel, petitioned the Court against the local council's interference with Nafar's freedom of artistic expression. Significantly, Nafar was not among the petitioners. The Court concurred with the petitioners, determining that the local council had no authority to interfere with Nafar's artistic content, and if there was concern regarding detrimental effects on public peace or security, police security should be provided for the event. Despite this ruling from an Israeli court, Nafar refused to perform in Umm al-Fahm. Instead, he accepted an invitation for dialogue with the conservative nonliberal forces within Umm al-Fahm council, a dialogue that resulted in reconciliation. I argue that Nafar's decision, as a liberal subject to choose dialogue with non-liberal forces in Palestinian society embodies the conceptual foundations of post-secularism, which extend beyond the binary of liberal/non liberal divisions and binaries and pave the way for internal dialogue between religious and secular actors. It constructs a platform for liberal subjects in Palestinian society to be heard in the public Palestinian sphere, providing social and political alternatives to the violent authority of Israeli law.

declarations.funderStatement: The author would like to thank the Core Research Grant (Grant No. CRG/2023/009012) issued to him under the SERB scheme of Anusandhan National Research Foundation. The funding support has helped him enormously with the research outcome.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the characterizations of equilibrium in economies with public projects. Public goods, as discussed by Mas-Colell (1980), are modeled as elements of an abstract set lacking a unified ordering structure. We introduce the concepts of cost share equilibrium for such economies, where the private commodity space is a (possibly nonseparable) Banach lattice. Within this framework, we present two distinct characterizations of cost share equilibria via the veto power of the grand coalition in economies featuring finitely many agents. The first characterization involves allocations that are Aubin non-dominated, while the second establishes that an allocation is a cost share equilibrium if and only if it cannot be dominated by the grand coalition, where domination is considered under specific perturbations of initial endowments.

title: Tell Me You Have a Plan! Insider Trade Signals from Firms Undergoing Corporate Downsizing
affiliations: Florida International University, Mississippi State University and Miami University of Ohio - Department of Finance

detail.title: Tell Me You Have a Plan! Insider Trade Signals from Firms Undergoing Corporate Downsizing
detail.abstract: Firms routinely reduce their employee headcount in response to competitive and economic pressures. The effectiveness of downsizing appears mixed as firms enjoy positive excess returns but also increased delisting and default likelihoods, consistent with compensating investors for additional risk. We explore insider trading activity as a signal of firm downsizing effectiveness. While insiders purchase more and sell fewer shares when firms downsize workforces, we focus on the downsizing group. Exploiting heterogeneity within downsizing firms, we find that the excess returns observed in downsizing firms are concentrated in firms where insiders purchase shares. Further, insider purchases are followed by lower future delisting likelihoods and financial distress in downsizing firms. Finally, we observe that insider purchases at downsizing firms are more prominent when trades are easily observable. Our results are consistent with insiders intentionally providing costly, credible signals about corporate executives' plan for firm improvement following downsizing.

title: Moral philosophy and archetypes in the symbolic cohesion of the story of simon the fool
affiliations: EDUKIVOTOS and Independent

detail.title: Moral philosophy and archetypes in the symbolic cohesion of the story of simon the fool
detail.abstract: This study explores the moralizing value of Rafael Pombo’s tale Simón el Bobito as a vehicle for ethical formation and social control in Colombia. It examines the “anti-villain” figure as an ambivalent protector who, through fear, seeks to safeguard the common good, in dialogue with Machiavelli’s and Hobbes’ theories on the ethics of fear. The analysis shows how the narrative combines humor, mockery, and punishment as collective pedagogies reinforcing social cohesion and order, transcending its childish tone toward a normative and ecological function.

detail.abstract: This article offers a critical review of State Transformation and Chinese Foreign Policy (Jones & Hameiri, 2021), a book that makes an important contribution by demonstrating how fragmentation, decentralisation, and internationalisation shape China’s foreign policy. Empirically rich and conceptually innovative, the text highlights institutional pluralism within the Chinese party-state. However, its explanatory framework reveals several limitations. It tends to overstate incoherence and dysfunction, underestimates the adaptive capacity of the Chinese Communist Party to reassert discipline through mechanisms such as cadre rotation, ideological campaigns, and digital surveillance, and relies predominantly on qualitative evidence without sufficient methodological triangulation. Most critically, the book neglects the decisive role of digital and algorithmic infrastructures—big data, artificial intelligence, and platform governance— that now underpin both domestic legitimacy and external influence. By addressing these omissions, this critique advances the case for a more multidimensional, mixed-methods approach that integrates institutional analysis with the digital–algorithmic turn. At a time of intensifying U.S.–China–Russia rivalry, such frameworks are essential to avoid misinterpretations that could exacerbate global instability and to open pathways for deeper research into China’s evolving state power and global role.

detail.abstract: With the rapid advancement of generative AI, multimodal models are poised to redefine the capabilities of intelligent transportation systems (ITS) and smart city applications. Traditional smart mobility management relies on large volumes of diverse traffic data-from roadside sensors, IoT-connected infrastructure, automated and connected vehicles (CAVs), and various simulation tools-making data fusion, simulation coupling, and predictive analytics complex and resource-intensive. This book chapter explores the potential of developing an AI foundation model for smart mobility through a unified multimodal generative AI architecture. We begin by presenting a forward-looking review of representative traffic and CAV datasets, highlighting their multimodal nature, including time series, geospatial trajectories, visual inputs, and textual data-which underpin current ITS implementations. We then examine the emerging capabilities of multimodal generative AI models to synthesize, interpret, and generate complex mobility insights from heterogeneous sources such as traffic signals, roadside sensors (e.g., loop detector and CCTV cameras), onboard data from connected vehicles (e.g., GPS, video, LiDAR), and crowdsourcing platforms. We explore the promise of training foundation models on transportation-relevant multimodal datasets to enable more adaptive, autonomous, and context-aware decision-making in urban mobility. By bridging fragmented data infrastructures with state-of-the-art generative AI architectures such as Vision-and-Language Transformer (ViLTs) and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), and emerging architectural paradigm, such as the Mixture of experts (MoE), we propose a multipurpose framework that employs a single unified AI architecture to (a) enable more accurate and comprehensive simulation and prediction of traffic through the fusion of multimodal data from ITS and CAVs, and (b) automate smart mobility management and system optimization tasks, from operational planning to public engagement. This paradigm shift offers a more scalable, unified, and maintainable approach to overcoming data silos and task-specific limitations, paving the way for more intelligent, responsive, efficient, and resilient transportation systems and vehicle technology of the future.

title: Voluntary Standards for Business and Human Rights: Reviewing and Categorizing the Field

detail.title: Voluntary Standards for Business and Human Rights: Reviewing and Categorizing the Field
detail.abstract: This chapter reviews the emerging landscape of voluntary standards in the business and human rights field. I start by defining ‘voluntary standards’, and I show how this type of regulation differs from legal sanctions and social norms. Next, I introduce a taxonomy to classify the landscape of standards for business and human rights. The taxonomy distinguishes standards based on their mode of governance as well as purpose. The following section reviews literature on voluntary standards and distinguishes between scholarly work on input to standard setting, the institutionalization of standards, and their impact (the “3Is”). Finally, this chapter outlines selected research topics that are either part of the contemporary debate on voluntary standards or reflect exciting research opportunities for future scholarly work.

title: Bringing Sustainability into the Boardroom - Structure, Mindset, Competencies
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School

detail.title: Bringing Sustainability into the Boardroom - Structure, Mindset, Competencies
detail.abstract: This chapter discusses how boards can integrate sustainability discussions into their decisions. I start by highlighting several rationales for why boards should engage with the sustainability agenda, ranging from legal arguments to reflections on value creation and improved investor relations. The following sections identify and discuss three issues which support the uptake of sustainability in the boardroom: (1) the structures that support the integration of sustainability into the boardroom, (2) the mindset with which boards approach sustainability discussions, and (3) the ESG-related competencies that directors should either have or develop. Reflecting on these issues helps boards to develop the right infrastructure to ensure adequate oversight of a firm's environmental, social, and governance (ESG) strategy.

detail.title: From Closed-Loop Supply Chains to Circular Ecosystems: Circular Business Models in the Dutch Microelectronics Industry

declarations.funderStatement: This research was carried out as part of the project Circular Circuits (P20-13) of the Netherlands Organization for Scientific Research.

detail.abstract: Rising resource scarcity and environmental pollution underscore the urgency for sustainable development. While technological innovations in circularity emerge rapidly, the practical implementation of Circular Business Models (CBMs) remains challenging. The Circular Economy (CE) requires cross-value-chain collaboration, demanding stakeholders co-create value within the ecosystem. Recent CE initiatives increasingly target entire business ecosystems, emphasising collaborative engagement. Yet, much of the existing literature continues to concentrate on individual products, firms, or industries, overlooking the complex interdependencies among stakeholders and offering limited empirical insights at the ecosystem level. This research addresses these gaps by empirically investigating how CBM development in the business ecosystem works, utilising an embedded case study of the Dutch microelectronics industry, including 18 stakeholders inside this ecosystem, such as manufacturers, repair service providers and recyclers. Our findings show diverse CBM categories within multiple firms and address the supply chain interconnections from an ecosystem perspective. Additionally, our study identifies key enablers (e.g., regulatory mandates, data transparency enhancement) and barriers (e.g., high operational costs, supply chain complexities, limited consumer acceptance) to achieving the circularity of an ecosystem. Ultimately, different stakeholders in the same business ecosystem can achieve broader sustainability goals with a systematic collaboration mindset. Our study advances both academic understanding and practical capabilities in ecosystem-level CBM development. We can provide insights for industries and policymakers, enabling them to systematically address barriers, leverage drivers, and foster sustainable value creation in a collaborative ecosystem.

detail.abstract: This study examines the changing nature of markets by comparing classic views with modern behavioural dynamics. Traditionally, markets have been viewed as organised areas where people make decisions based on logic and classical economic ideas. But the rise of digital technology, globalisation, and ideas from behavioural economics have changed how markets work, which goes against some of the basic ideas that people have about them. The study analyses the impact of consumer psychology, information asymmetry, and technological platforms on contemporary market outcomes through interdisciplinary frameworks. Case examples from both physical and digital marketplaces demonstrate a departure from conventional models, underscoring the complexity and adaptability of contemporary economic relationships. The study provides a comprehensive knowledge of market transition and its consequences for policy, legislation, and economic theory through a critical analysis of these shifts.

detail.abstract:
This paper proposes Organizational Emotional Materiality (OEM) framework that specifies how emotions influence organizational value through three distinct pathways: Emotion-Decision pathway, Emotion-Social capital pathway and Emotion-Market signaling pathway. It integrates Affective Events Theory, Social Exchange Theory, Emotion Regulation Theory and organizational capability perspectives to develop five testable propositions that advance understanding of when, how and why emotions become strategically material for organizations. The OEM framework addresses gaps in organizational behavior literature by providing a systematic theoretical model linking micro-level emotional processes to macro-level organizational outcomes, while specifying boundary conditions and measurement considerations for empirical validation. The theoretical contribution lies in reconceptualizing emotions from peripheral organizational factors to measurable strategic resources that systematically influence competitive advantage through identifiable causal mechanisms. The paper offers evidence-based recommendations for embedding emotional awareness into strategic management while acknowledging the risks of dysfunctional emotional manipulation.

title: Climate Change, Water Governance, and Rural Poverty: A Political Economy Perspective on the Teesta Basin

detail.title: Climate Change, Water Governance, and Rural Poverty: A Political Economy Perspective on the Teesta Basin
detail.abstract: The Teesta River (*Teesta Nodi*), a lifeline for millions in northern Bangladesh, has become emblematic of the intersection between climate change, water governance, and rural poverty. This paper adopts a political economy perspective to explore how declining water availability, poor governance structures, and regional geopolitics exacerbate environmental vulnerabilities and socioeconomic marginalization in Rangpur and Kurigram districts. Using secondary literature, government policy documents, and political economy frameworks, the paper argues that the Teesta water crisis is not only an environmental problem but also a governance failure with deep political roots. Policy recommendations highlight the need for hydro-diplomacy with India, climate-resilient agricultural strategies, and decentralized governance reforms to address poverty traps in the Teesta Basin.

detail.abstract: This report provides a comprehensive analysis of Airbus SE within the context of the global commercial aircraft manufacturing industry, characterised by its enduring duopoly with Boeing. The study begins with an industry overview, employing Porter's Five Forces to assess the competitive environment, before focusing on Airbus's business strategy, diversified portfolio, and sustainability-driven vision. A comparative examination of Airbus and Boeing follows, using horizontal and vertical analyses of financial statements (2022-2024) to highlight Airbus's operational resilience against Boeing's instability, shaped by reputational and structural challenges. Ratio analysis further underscores Airbus's strengths in efficiency, liquidity, and solvency, in contrast to Boeing's prolonged difficulties in cash conversion, leverage, and profitability. Decomposition of return on equity reveals that Airbus leverages financial structure effectively to deliver above-average shareholder returns, whereas Boeing's negative equity position distorts conventional measures. The intrinsic valuation, based on a Discounted Cash Flow framework incorporating a conservative WACC (7.06%) and long-term growth assumptions, estimates Airbus's intrinsic share price at €119.84. Compared with a prevailing market price of €154.90, the findings suggest modest overvaluation, possibly explained by market optimism, strategic intangibles, and sentiment-driven pricing. Overall, the report illustrates Airbus's position as a financially robust, innovation-oriented leader well placed to capitalise on the rising global demand for sustainable aviation, while also noting the limitations and behavioural factors that influence divergence between intrinsic and market valuations.

detail.abstract: The term "flow-sizing" in healthcare systems refers to the strategic operations management of critical care resources in response to emergencies, adjusting resource availability to meet fluctuating demand. Conventional optimization and static queueing formulations struggle in this setting because objectives are non-compensatory and evolve over time, whereas the effects of policy levers are nonlinear, interrelated and lagged. We propose a novel framework that combines a multiplicative utility function with machine learning (ML) techniques to evaluate and support critical care capacity planning. The proposed framework relies upon: i) a time-dependent utility function based on hard mortality data and key explanatory features using a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) model, ii) domain-informed capacity attributes through logistic-based univariate utility functions, and iii) a calibration of their relative weights using a module that combines differential evolution with deep reinforcement learning. Using the Greek healthcare system during COVID-19 as a case study, the framework reproduces mortality-linked dynamics and identifies high-agility and targeted flow-sizing policies that consistently deliver higher aggregate utility than status-quo triggers, initiate earlier capacity pivots as risk escalates and remain robust across multiple what-if scenarios. The framework captures the structural complexity and temporal dynamics of critical care under strain, providing interpretable, adaptable, evidence-based decision support grounded in real data.

detail.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Applied Relational Healing™ (ARH), a prevention-first theoretical framework that integrates prevention science, relational development theory, and human-centered leadership principles to address systemic trauma before crisis occurs. Current trauma-informed approaches remain predominantly reactive, focusing on symptom management after harm has occurred rather than building trauma-resistant organizational cultures. Drawing on ecological systems theory (Bronfenbrenner, 1979), social learning theory (Bandura, 1977), and contemporary trauma research (van der Kolk, 2014; Maté & Maté, 2022), ARH proposes a three-pillar sequential model: Prevention-First Foundation, Relational Development Core, and Human-Centered Leadership Integration. This framework addresses three critical gaps in current approaches: timing (interventions arrive post-crisis), scope (individual focus misses systemic dynamics), and depth (surface awareness fails to build relational infrastructure). ARH theorizes that organizations implementing this sequential framework would experience enhanced relational capacity, reduced crisis incidents, and self-sustaining trauma prevention systems. This paper articulates the theoretical foundation, core propositions, and research agenda for empirically testing the ARH framework in organizational settings.

detail.abstract: This paper presents comprehensive empirical validation of the Current Risk Detection Suite (CIX), a deterministic analytical framework operationalizing the theoretical constructs of systemic resonance, coherence, and feedback introduced in the Balantium framework (Klemarczyk, 2025). Unlike conventional risk models that rely on stochastic assumptions or machine learning approaches, CIX employs field-theoretic transformations to quantify systemic coherence decay as a precursor to financial instability. Through comprehensive backtesting across 25 years of market data encompassing eleven major financial crises-including the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, the 2010 Flash Crash, the 2018 Volmageddon event, and the 2020 COVID-19 market collapse-CIX demonstrated exceptional predictive performance. The system achieved lead times ranging from 75 to 250 days (mean = 147 days, = 48), Sharpe ratios between 1.018 and 5.424 (mean = 2.31), Sortino ratios from 0.682 to 7.070 (mean = 3.12), and Calmar ratios spanning 2.398 to 59.281 (mean = 18.7). Classification metrics revealed precision rates of 59.5%-95.2% (mean = 72.8%) with recall rates of 3.4%-78.1% (mean = 44.6%) across diverse market conditions. Monte Carlo validation (n = 1,001 trials) and walk-forward analysis confirmed statistical significance (p < 0.001) and out-of-sample robustness. These results substantially exceed conventional risk management benchmarks and provide empirical support for coherence-based systemic risk detection.

detail.abstract: Patents are widely recognized as a key driver of R&D and commercialization in the biotechnology industry, particularly for startups. In 2008, a team of researchers at the University of California, Berkeley (including this chapter's author) conducted the most comprehensive survey to date on the role of patenting among biotech and other startups. The Berkeley Patent Survey asked senior managers about their motivations for seeking (and not seeking) patents, the number of patents and applications they had filed and acquired, the impact of third-party patents on their R&D and commercialization efforts, and their reliance on patents compared with other forms of intellectual property. In general, biotech startups reported obtaining a very large number of patents, primarily to prevent others from copying their products and services. In addition, they reported that patents were useful for raising financing, negotiating licensing deals, and bargaining during acquisition negotiations. Biotech startups generally did not perceive third-party patents as particularly problematic to their own R&D and commercialization efforts. Patents and trade secrets were the most dominant forms of intellectual property used by biotech companies, with patents slightly edging out trade secrets. Between 2008 and 2025, several other researchers have performed empirical studies on the role of patenting among biotech startups, largely with similar findings to the Berkeley Patent Survey. This chapter explores the findings of those studies against the backdrop of the Berkeley Survey and changes in the law and advances in technology since 2008, suggesting avenues for further research.

title: Opportunity or Threat? Rank-and-File Employees’ Survival Needs and the Differential Mechanics of Generative AI Acceptance
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Shanghai University of Engineering Science, Shanghai Lixin University of Accounting and Finance and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Opportunity or Threat? Rank-and-File Employees’ Survival Needs and the Differential Mechanics of Generative AI Acceptance
detail.abstract: The application of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) at the rank-and-file level has intensified employee anxieties about job survival related to the widespread application of AI. Yet, the existing research has yet to explore the mechanism of technological acceptance from the perspective of employee psycho-emotional “survival needs,” and there is corresponding lack of dynamic stress assessments. This study integrates the technology acceptance model (TAM) with the cognitive appraisal theory of stress (CATS), treating the large-scale application of GenAI as an employee stressor. Based on empirical data from 291 rank-and-file employees, this study constructs a primary-secondary dual-stage framework to examine employees’ path to acceptance as driven by these basic workplace survival needs. The results show that in the primary appraisal stage, technical compatibility (TCO) is perceived as an opportunity, significantly enhancing perceived usefulness (PU) and perceived ease of use (PEOU). In contrast, technical frustration (TF) is perceived as a threat, inhibiting the development of both PU and PEOU. In the secondary appraisal stage, job demand-control (JDC) and perceived organizational support (POS) effectively transform threats into acceptance motivation by providing survival assurance resources. Moreover, self-efficacy (SE) significantly strengthens the conversion of PU/PEOU into behavioral intention (BI), ultimately driving use behavior (UB). These conclusions indicate that survival needs are the driving force behind rank-and-file employees' acceptance of GenAI applications. The characteristics of the technology characteristics trigger primary survival threat appraisals, while organizational resources can be converted to survival assurances through secondary appraisals, thereby activating the TAM cognitive pathway. This paper also discusses the theoretical and practical implications of these findings, as well as potential directions for future research.

detail.abstract: The origins of credit statistics by economic sector (Statistiche sul credito per rami di attività) form a crucial part of the history of official statistics in Italy. In the way they were conceived and in the institutional context in which they were developed, they represent a significant episode for at least two complementary reasons: they enabled a systematic encounter between statistics and economic analysis – something rare in the Italian tradition – and they gave rise to a form of statistical production that was autonomous from political power, and thus stable, reliable, and enduring. Within the context of the fascist dictatorship, the creation of the Research Department at the Bank of Italy contributed to making the institution a stable technostructure over time – one capable of ensuring methodological consistency in its statistical outputs. It allowed to establish a technostructure that did not merely carry out the will of the regime, but rather drew on a degree of theoretical and, to some extent, organizational autonomy.

detail.abstract: This research aims to evaluate the quality of Automated Teller Machine (ATM) services offered by the Commercial Bank of Ethiopia (CBE) in Addis Ababa. The primary objective is to analyze customer perceptions and satisfaction levels regarding CBE's ATM services, ultimately striving to enhance service quality and boost customer retention. The study provides a comprehensive understanding of user experiences by examining key factors such as reliability, responsiveness, ease of use, security and privacy, convenience, and overall service fulfillment. A mixed-methods approach was employed to collect data, incorporating both surveys and interviews with customers in Addis Ababa. The findings highlight the significant role of improving ATM service quality in fostering customer satisfaction and loyalty. This study not only provides actionable insights for CBE to improve its service offerings, but it also proposes tactics for improving the whole banking experience for customers in Ethiopia. The study included 384 respondents chosen using Kothari's (2004) sample size selection technique, with a fantastic return rate of 93.75% from 360 successfully returned questionnaires, which formed the foundation of the analysis and interpretation. The study found that overall customer satisfaction obtained a modest rating (mean score: 3.5984), indicating area for development in terms of ease and overall satisfaction with CBE services. To improve the CBE's ATM services in Addis Ababa, constant monitoring, user-friendly design, high security, and increased accessibility through better placement and support should be addressed.

detail.abstract: The notion of accountability is understood as the duty to provide an account of the actions for which organisations are held responsible in the eyes of their stakeholders, or, more generically, as the giving and demanding of reasons for conduct. It should come as no surprise, hence, that a certain narrative capacity, an ability to narrate and enable audience comprehension is to be found at the core of accounting. The resulting magic - through which words and numbers become translated into objects, people, and actions, and then back into words and numbers - has long since captured the attention of accounting scholars, and the extant literature has established that accounting narratives do indeed use stories, metaphors, and attributions within their numbers. Nevertheless, as narrative accounting becomes an ever increasingly dominant presence in current practices with the increasing emphasis on impact and connected issues which lack clear, standard measurements, old issues resurface and new ones emerge. The paper proposes an alternative methodological approach, considering narrative reports as stories and analysing them through tools from narratology, to answer some of these open questions: how are contemporary accounts of impact constructed from a narratological perspective? Which narrative devices might be conducive to the production of good, meaningful stories?

detail.abstract: The purpose of this study was to investigate the effect of self-regulation on test anxiety: academic achievement and metacognition among secondary school students. Three research questions guided the study and two hypotheses tested at 0.05 level of significant. The study adopted a pre-test post-test control quasi experimental design. The study was conducted using 100 students. A study group was selected purposively in accordance with the objectives of the study and a multiple-choice test comprised of 50 items was developed to test participants' levels of knowledge before and after the experimentation. The internal consistency reliability of the test was estimated using the KR-20 formula, with a result of 0.73 and the validity was equally established. The pre-test and post-test scores of the students in both the experimental and control groups were analyzed using descriptive statistics and compared using both paired and independent samples t tests and ANCOVA. Pre-test results suggested no significant difference between the learning levels of test anxious students in the experimental and control groups. The experimental group was then educated on self-regulation and metacognition before teaching. At the end of the teaching process, a comparison between post-test scores revealed that students in the experimental group had significantly higher scores than those in the control group. It was recommended among others that self-regulation and metacognition be used in higher institutions as well, and should be included in guidance and counseling programs in secondary schools and considered most important among others.

title: The Impact of Disruptions of Supply Chains on American Multinational Companies

detail.abstract: The objective of the thesis is to understand and analyze the impact of disruptions of supply chains on American companies. When there is a supply chain disruption, companies react by changes in how they operate. Sometimes these changes are so subtle that they go unnoticed even by employees. The employees referred to here are not the C-suite employees but regular managers, directors, and line workers. A few times, these changes are not impactful enough to dent or boost the company’s stock price but surely impact individual employees’ lives. Companies, which in reality are only businesses, have a need to maintain a certain level of profitability or revenue reporting. A change in those figures for the worse may unnerve the confidence of the board of directors. To prevent that from happening, company operating officers look for ways to fix the situation. It can be in the form of pay or personnel cuts. These actions slip through the cracks because the company’s stock market report does not usually mention them. The only way to gather information is to interview company employees - almost always anonymously and use a qualitative analysis tool to analyze the results. That analysis can give valuable insights into the impact of disruptions of supply chains on these companies. In this thesis, the researcher uses the qualitative method of research to delve deep to understand the impact of supply chain disruptions on American multinational companies. Qualitative primary research was done via one-to-one interviews and email surveys. Interviews were done via the popular video calling software Zoom and recorded. Recordings were transcribed and fed into the leading qualitative analysis software –Atlas.ti and analyzed. The email surveys were also analyzed using Atlas.ti. The results of the analysis gave valuable private insights into the impact of supply chain disruption on American multinational companies. Secondary research was done utilizing ManipalGlobalNxt’s extensive online library of peer-reviewed theses and using sources from the Internet. Secondary research provided insightful information that closely corroborated with the analysis from primary research. A literature review done prior to both the primary and secondary research by the author provided a solid base for the research. Using classical qualitative research theories, the author triangulated the research into impactful insights that can benefit both businesses and researchers for decades to come and provide a valuable starting point for more research.

title: Regime Change as a Weapon- The Silent Siege of South Asia
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Regime Change as a Weapon- The Silent Siege of South Asia
detail.abstract: Over the past decade, India’s political landscape has increasingly been shaped by forces that go beyond organic domestic dissent, reflecting patterns of coordinated regime change experiments and destabilisation strategies. Narratives around corruption, caste polarisation, farmer unrest, and digital disinformation have been amplified through global media platforms, external NGOs, and transnational funding networks. These efforts, while ostensibly spontaneous, bear resemblance to tactics witnessed in other South Asian contexts, such as Sri Lanka, Bangladesh, and Nepal, where regime change movements achieved significant political upheaval. In India, episodes such as the Citizenship Amendment Act (CAA) protests and the 2020–21 farmer demonstrations illustrate how legitimate grievances were rapidly internationalised and reframed as existential threats to Indian democracy. While these pressures have not resulted in regime collapse, they represent sustained attempts to test India’s resilience, weaken its political coherence, and constrain its ascent as a stable global power. Anchored in B.R. Ambedkar’s insight that democracy extends beyond governance to social organisation, this analysis highlights how India is subjected to a silent siege that blends protest, perception management, and international influence in order to redirect its trajectory.

detail.abstract: This research paper introduces Cognitive Mirror Syndrome (CMS) - a novel framework for understanding how AI systems create self-reinforcing cognitive loops that gradually separate both humans and artificial systems from objective reality. Unlike traditional concerns about AI bias or dependence, CMS describes a unique phenomenon where AI systems become cognitive mirrors that reflect increasingly distorted versions of human thought patterns back to users, creating a closed feedback system with no external reality verification. Through analysis of current AI deployment patterns and cognitive psychology research, this paper establishes CMS as a distinct and urgent challenge requiring immediate intervention to preserve human cognitive autonomy and societal connection to objective truth.

title: No Papers Please: Anglophone Antipathy to National ID Cards

detail.title: No Papers Please: Anglophone Antipathy to National ID Cards
detail.abstract: Most of the countries in the world today, including all but six of the members of the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development, have some form of national identification (ID) card or a national ID system. These six countries also happen to be all "Anglophone" countries. But while it may be true that the Anglophone world is an outlier with respect to its reluctance to embrace national IDs, this hesitance is not absolute and can vary depending on the location and on the time. The clearest example is the UK, which had a national ID system for 13 years and is on the verge of re-launching one in 2025 due in part to public support for a national ID recovering to over a majority of the population. This shows that while a certain subset of the Anglophone population will always be skeptical of national IDs, the majority appears to be willing to at least consider and even embrace such IDs if sufficient justification exists, such as a national security or illegal immigration crisis. Given the historic nature of a national ID being re-introduced into the UK from a legal and political perspective, this article overviews the history of national IDs in the four largest Anglophone countries and attempts to explain why they are gradually diverging in their approaches to national IDs in spite of their shared colonial ancestry.

title: The effect of Public Financial Management on Treasury Single Account in the Federal Inland Revenue Service, Maiduguri, Borno State

detail.title: The effect of Public Financial Management on Treasury Single Account in the Federal Inland Revenue Service, Maiduguri, Borno State

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I hereby declare that, I have no personal or financial interest in the organisation that the study was carried out.
declarations.funderStatement: This study was funded by Nigerias Tertiardy Education Trust Fund

detail.abstract: This study investigates the effect of Public Financial Management (PFM) components-Revenue Remittance, Cash Management Effectiveness, and Staff Perceptions of Operations-on the Treasury Single Account (TSA) in the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS) office within Maiduguri Metropolis, Borno State. Guided by Agency Theory and New Public Management (NPM) Theory, the study hypothesized that PFM tools would significantly influence TSA outcomes by reducing information asymmetries, improving accountability, and enhancing efficiency. Data were analyzed using Generalized Least Squares (GLS) regression following diagnostic tests for heteroscedasticity, Hausman specification, and Lagrangian Multiplier (LM) effects. The results revealed that although the PFM variables were positively related to TSA outcomes, their effects were statistically insignificant at the 5% level. The regression model explained only 11% of the variation in TSA implementation, indicating that 89% of the variance was attributable to factors outside the model. These findings suggest that while PFM tools conceptually align with TSA objectives, their practical impact remains limited within the Maiduguri FIRS office. The study concludes that TSA implementation requires more than procedural tools; it demands institutional alignment, robust ICT infrastructure, effective monitoring mechanisms, and stronger compliance enforcement. Policymakers and managers should therefore focus on capacity building, integration of financial management information systems, and harmonization of revenue processes to maximize the effectiveness of TSA reforms and strengthen Nigeria's fiscal discipline.
